domain.title: GPU Kernels & Compilers
domain.tag: CUDA · warps · tensor cores · FlashAttention · Triton · CUTLASS · torch.compile
domain.why: Every AI model you've heard of ultimately runs as code written specifically for graphics processors (GPUs), and the number of people who can write that code well is small — which makes it one of the most valuable and visible skills in this whole field. It's also unusually honest as a skill: either your code runs close to the hardware's real speed limit or it doesn't, and a performance measurement doesn't lie or negotiate.

sections.note: Hardware facts live in domain 04. This section is about the abstraction you actually type.

concepts.t: Grid, block, thread: the launch triple

L0.cloze: A launch is `k<<<{{c1::grid}}, {{c2::block}}, smem_bytes, stream>>>(...)`; the grid size is computed by {{c3::ceil-division}} so that every element is covered.

concepts.L1: A kernel launch names a grid of blocks and a block of threads, up to three dimensions each. Blocks are scheduled onto SMs in an order you cannot control and cannot depend on; threads inside a block share an SM, shared memory, and a barrier.
concepts.L2: The block is the unit of guaranteed co-residency; the grid is not. Two blocks may run concurrently, back to back, or on different SMs, so a kernel that requires block 0 to finish before block 1 starts is a deadlock waiting for the wrong launch shape. Grid-wide sync needs cooperative launch or a second kernel.
concepts.L3: Ceil-division is why the bounds guard exists. For $n = 1000$ and 256 threads per block, $\lceil 1000/256 \rceil = 4$ blocks and $4 \times 256 = 1024$ threads, so 24 threads have $i \geq n$ and must not touch memory. The integer idiom `(n + 255) / 256` is $\lfloor (n + b - 1)/b \rfloor$, exact for all $n \geq 0$ short of overflow. Blocks are independent by design: the hardware retires a block's resources the moment its last warp exits, then launches the next waiting block onto that SM, which is what lets one binary run on a 20-SM laptop part and a 132-SM H100 without recompilation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel is launched with block size {b} over n = {n} elements using ceil-division. How many blocks launch, and how many threads have index i >= n? Answer with the number of blocks.
L4.answer: blocks = ceil(n/b); idle = blocks*b - n. For b=256, n=1000: 4 blocks, 24 idle threads.
L4.explanation: blocks $= \lceil n/b \rceil$ and idle $= b\lceil n/b \rceil - n$. Checks: (256,1000) gives 4 and 24; (128,100000) gives 782 and 96; (512,65537) gives 129 and 511. Every idle thread must be turned off by the bounds guard, not by luck.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel writes out[blockIdx.x] then reads out[blockIdx.x - 1], assuming block {a} ran before block {b}. What is wrong?
L4.answer: Block execution order is unspecified. There is no ordering or visibility guarantee between blocks in one launch, so the read may see uninitialised memory.
L4.explanation: Only threads within a block have a barrier. Cross-block ordering requires a separate kernel launch, a cooperative grid-wide launch, or an explicit atomically-published flag with fences, and even then only if the blocks are co-resident.

concepts.t: Warps: the unit that actually executes

L0.cloze: A warp is {{c1::32}} threads issued together; a block of 100 threads costs {{c2::4}} warps, and the last warp runs with {{c3::28}} lanes masked off.

concepts.L1: The hardware schedules warps, not threads. A warp is 32 lanes that share one instruction pointer per issue on pre-Volta parts and one convergence-tracked program counter set after. Occupancy, divergence, coalescing and shuffle all quantise to 32.
concepts.L2: Block sizes that are not multiples of 32 waste whole lanes silently. A 48-thread block occupies two warps and permanently masks 16 lanes: you pay full scheduling and register cost for 16 threads that compute nothing. Nothing in the profiler labels this an error; it just shows as low achieved throughput.
concepts.L3: Warps per block is $\lceil T/32 \rceil$ for block size $T$. At $T=100$ that is 4 warps, 128 lane-slots, of which 28 are dead: 21.9 percent of issue slots wasted before the kernel does anything. Registers are allocated per warp, so those dead lanes also consume register file. From Volta onward each thread has its own program counter and the scheduler can interleave diverged paths, which fixes some lock-free idioms but does not make divergence free: the warp still issues once per taken path. `__syncwarp()` exists precisely because implicit reconvergence stopped being guaranteed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A block has {T} threads. How many warps does it occupy and how many lane-slots are wasted? Answer with the number of warps.
L4.answer: warps = ceil(T/32); wasted = 32*warps - T. T=100 gives 4 warps, 28 wasted.
L4.explanation: Checks: T=100 gives 4 warps and 28 wasted; T=48 gives 2 and 16; T=256 gives 8 and 0; T=33 gives 2 and 31. Only multiples of 32 waste nothing, which is why 128, 256 and 512 are the block sizes you see everywhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need {T} threads of real work per block. Which block size do you launch?
options: Exactly T, so no thread is idle
The next multiple of 32 at or above T, with a bounds guard
Always 1024, the maximum
L4.answer: The next multiple of 32 at or above T, with a bounds guard
L4.explanation: Launching exactly T does not avoid the partial warp; the hardware rounds up regardless, so you get the waste and an odd shape. Always launching 1024 caps occupancy through registers and shared memory. Round to 32 and guard.

concepts.t: The memory hierarchy you can address

L0.body:
float  r;                      // register: per-thread, ~1 cycle
__shared__ float s[1024];      // per-block SRAM, ~30 cycle, banked
extern __shared__ float dyn[]; // size given as 3rd launch arg
__constant__ float c[256];     // broadcast-optimised, 64 KB total
float* g;                      // global: HBM, hundreds of cycles
__device__ float dev_static[N];
L0.cloze: Per-thread storage is {{c1::registers}}; per-block SRAM is `{{c2::__shared__}}`; dynamic shared memory is sized by the {{c3::third}} launch argument.

concepts.L1: Five address spaces you write by name: registers, shared, constant, local (spilled registers, physically in global), and global. Latency and capacity move in opposite directions across them, and the whole craft of kernel writing is deciding which data lives where.
concepts.L2: Local memory is not local. It is a per-thread slice of global DRAM used for register spills and any array a thread indexes dynamically, so `float tmp[8]; tmp[i] = ...` with a runtime `i` quietly moves a hot array off-chip. Only compile-time-constant indices keep an array in registers.
concepts.L3: Registers are the only storage with no addressing cost, which is why register tiling beats shared-memory tiling. Shared memory is SRAM on the SM, banked 32 ways, and is the only user-managed level: you decide what is cached and when it is evicted. Constant memory is a 64 KB region with a small per-SM cache tuned for the case where all 32 lanes read the same address, where it broadcasts in one transaction; if lanes read 32 different constant addresses it serialises. Global memory is HBM behind L2 and L1. On A100 (cc 8.0) an SM has 192 KB of combined L1 and shared, of which at most 164 KB is addressable as shared; on H100 (cc 9.0) the figure is 228 KB per SM and 227 KB per block.

L4.prompt_tpl: A thread declares `float acc[{n}];` and indexes it with a loop variable the compiler cannot unroll. Where does acc live and what does it cost?
L4.answer: In local memory, which is global DRAM. Every access is a hundreds-of-cycle round trip instead of a register read.
L4.explanation: Dynamic indexing forces the array out of the register file because registers are not addressable. Fix it with `#pragma unroll` on the loop and compile-time bounds, or restructure so each element gets its own named variable. `ncu` reports it as local memory traffic.

L4.prompt_tpl: On an SM with {kb} KB of shared memory available per SM, how many blocks each requesting {req} KB can be resident?
L4.answer: floor(kb/req). 164/48 gives 3 blocks; 164/32 gives 5; 228/48 gives 4; 100/16 gives 6.
L4.explanation: Shared memory is a hard per-SM budget and one of the three occupancy limiters. 164 KB with 48 KB blocks admits 3 blocks and strands 20 KB. Dropping the request to 32 KB admits 5 and strands 4 KB, which is usually the better trade.

concepts.t: Global index arithmetic and the bounds guard

L0.cloze: The canonical 1-D index is `blockIdx.x * {{c1::blockDim.x}} + threadIdx.x`, and it must be followed by `if (i < {{c2::n}})` because the grid is rounded {{c3::up}}.

concepts.L1: Index arithmetic maps the thread lattice onto the data. In 2-D the convention is x for the fastest-varying dimension so that consecutive `threadIdx.x` values touch consecutive addresses, which is exactly the condition for coalescing.
concepts.L2: Swapping row and col in the 2-D mapping is the single most common performance bug in a first kernel. `C[col*N + row]` is correct and eight times slower than `C[row*N + col]`, because now consecutive lanes stride by N and each lane needs its own memory transaction.
concepts.L3: Take a 2-D launch with a 32 by 8 block. With `col` from `threadIdx.x`, the 32 lanes of a warp have consecutive `col` and identical `row`, so their addresses `row*N + col` are 32 consecutive floats, 128 contiguous bytes: four 32-byte sectors, the minimum. With the mapping swapped, lane $j$ addresses $(\mathrm{col}_j) \cdot N + \mathrm{row}$ with $\mathrm{col}_j$ consecutive, so addresses are $N$ floats apart. For $N \geq 8$ every lane lands in a distinct 32-byte sector: 32 sectors, 1024 bytes fetched to use 128, an eightfold waste. The guard `if (i < n)` costs one predicated instruction and prevents the out-of-bounds write that would otherwise corrupt whatever the allocator put next.

L4.prompt_tpl: A warp reads a column of a row-major float matrix with N = {N}. How many 32-byte sectors does that warp touch, and how many bytes are fetched to deliver 128 useful bytes? Answer with the number of sectors the warp touches.
L4.answer: 32 sectors, 1024 bytes fetched for 128 useful: 8x waste (true for any N >= 8 floats).
L4.explanation: Lane $j$ addresses $j \cdot N \cdot 4$ bytes. Once $4N \geq 32$, no two lanes share a 32-byte sector, so the warp touches 32 sectors and moves $32 \times 32 = 1024$ bytes. The useful payload is $32 \times 4 = 128$ bytes, so 87.5 percent of the traffic is thrown away.

L4.prompt_tpl: This kernel runs correctly for n = {ok} but corrupts memory for n = {bad}: `int i = blockIdx.x*blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; y[i] = x[i];` launched with ceil-div grid and block 256. Explain.
L4.answer: The bounds guard is missing. It only appears correct when n is an exact multiple of the block size, so no thread has i >= n.
L4.explanation: With n = 1000 and block 256 the grid rounds to 4 blocks, 1024 threads, and threads 1000 to 1023 write past the end. The bug hides on power-of-two sizes, which is why it survives testing and fails in production.

concepts.t: Choosing a launch configuration: occupancy arithmetic in practice

L0.cloze: `{{c1::cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor}}` reports resident blocks; `-Xptxas {{c2::-v}}` prints per-thread registers; `{{c3::__launch_bounds__}}` tells the compiler the occupancy you want.

concepts.L1: Occupancy is resident warps over the hardware maximum, and three budgets cap it independently: registers per SM, shared memory per SM, and the block-count and thread-count ceilings. The binding one is whichever gives the smallest block residency.
concepts.L2: Maximum occupancy is not the goal. A register-tiled GEMM at 25 percent occupancy routinely beats a 100-percent-occupancy version, because the registers that cost occupancy are what create instruction-level parallelism. Occupancy only matters until you have enough parallelism to cover memory latency.
concepts.L3: On A100 (cc 8.0) an SM allows 2048 threads, 64 warps, 32 blocks, 65536 32-bit registers and up to 164 KB shared. Take 256 threads per block at 64 registers per thread: registers per block is $256 \times 64 = 16384$, so $\lfloor 65536/16384 \rfloor = 4$ blocks fit, giving 1024 threads, 32 warps, 50 percent occupancy. Recompile at 32 registers and $\lfloor 65536/8192 \rfloor = 8$ blocks fit: 2048 threads, 64 warps, 100 percent. Now add 48 KB of shared per block: $\lfloor 164/48 \rfloor = 3$ blocks, so shared memory becomes binding at 37.5 percent regardless of registers. The minimum across limiters wins, and `__launch_bounds__` trades registers for residency deliberately.

L4.prompt_tpl: On an SM with 65536 registers, 2048 max threads and 64 max warps: block size {T}, {R} registers per thread, {S} KB shared per block, 164 KB shared per SM. Give resident blocks and occupancy. Answer with the occupancy as a fraction.
L4.answer: blocks = min(65536//(T*R), 2048//T, 32, 164//S if S>0 else inf); occupancy = blocks*T/32/64.
L4.explanation: Checks: T=256, R=64, S=0 gives min(4, 8, 32) = 4 blocks, 32 warps, 50 percent. T=256, R=32, S=48 gives min(8, 8, 32, 3) = 3 blocks, 24 warps, 37.5 percent, shared-limited. T=128, R=40, S=16 gives min(12, 16, 32, 10) = 10 blocks, 40 warps, 62.5 percent.

L4.prompt_tpl: Kernel A runs at {a} percent occupancy, kernel B at {b} percent, and B is faster. Give the most likely reason.
L4.answer: B uses more registers per thread to hold a register tile, buying instruction-level parallelism and cutting memory traffic. Latency is already hidden, so extra warps buy nothing.
L4.explanation: Occupancy hides latency only up to the point where the memory system is saturated or the arithmetic pipe is full. Beyond that, fewer, fatter threads that reuse data in registers move less memory. This is exactly why cuBLAS-class GEMM kernels sit near 25 percent.

concepts.t: Function qualifiers, PTX and separate compilation

L0.cloze: A kernel is `{{c1::__global__}}` and must return `{{c2::void}}`; embedding `code=compute_90` ships {{c3::PTX}} so a future GPU can JIT it.

concepts.L1: `__global__` marks an entry point, `__device__` a device-side callee, `__host__ __device__` a function compiled for both. `nvcc` splits the file: host code goes to the host compiler, device code to PTX and then to SASS for each named architecture.
concepts.L2: A fatbinary can contain SASS for specific SMs and PTX for forward compatibility, and getting this wrong is a deployment failure, not a performance one. If you ship only `code=sm_80` and run on Hopper, the driver has no cubin and no PTX to JIT, and the launch fails with `no kernel image is available`.
concepts.L3: `arch=compute_XX` names the virtual PTX ISA; `code=sm_XX` names the real SASS target. `code=compute_XX` embeds the PTX itself, which the driver JITs at load time for any newer architecture, at a one-off compile cost that `CUDA_CACHE_PATH` amortises. This matters because SASS is not a stable interface: NVIDIA does not document it and changes encodings between generations, so `cuobjdump -sass` and `nvdisasm` are read-only tools. `-Xptxas -v` is the cheapest diagnostic in the toolchain: it prints registers per thread, shared bytes, constant bytes and, critically, spill stores and loads, which tell you the compiler ran out of registers before the profiler does.

L4.prompt_tpl: A binary built with only `-gencode arch=compute_{a},code=sm_{a}` is run on an sm_{b} device. What happens?
L4.answer: The launch fails with 'no kernel image is available for execution on the device' (cudaErrorNoKernelImageForDevice).
L4.explanation: SASS is not forward compatible across major architectures and the fatbinary carries no PTX to JIT from. Adding `-gencode arch=compute_80,code=compute_80` embeds PTX so the driver can compile at load time.

L4.prompt_tpl: `-Xptxas -v` reports {n} spill stores and {m} spill loads for your kernel. What does that mean and what do you do?
L4.answer: The compiler ran out of registers and moved variables to local memory, which is DRAM. Reduce live values, shrink the register tile, or raise the register cap with __launch_bounds__ or -maxrregcount.
L4.explanation: Spills convert register reads into hundreds-of-cycle global accesses inside the hot loop. They usually appear right after you enlarge a thread tile, and they are the reason a bigger tile can be slower than a smaller one.

prereqs: Grid, block, thread: the launch triple

L0.cloze: `cudaGetLastError()` catches {{c1::launch}} errors; an illegal memory access only surfaces at the next {{c2::synchronising}} call; timing uses `cudaEvent{{c3::ElapsedTime}}`.

concepts.L1: Kernel launches are asynchronous: the call returns after enqueueing. So a kernel's error does not appear at the launch site. `cudaGetLastError` catches configuration failures; runtime faults surface at the next synchronising call, often inside unrelated code.
concepts.L2: Timing a kernel with host clocks around the launch measures the enqueue, not the kernel, and reports microseconds for work that takes milliseconds. CUDA events are recorded in the stream and timed by the device, which is why `cudaEventElapsedTime` is the only correct in-process timer.
concepts.L3: The runtime keeps one sticky error per thread; `cudaGetLastError` reads and clears it. Because faults are detected by the SM long after the host moved on, an illegal address in kernel A is routinely reported by the `cudaMemcpy` after kernel B, which is why `compute-sanitizer` exists. Streams give ordering: operations in one stream are ordered relative to each other and unordered relative to other streams. The legacy default stream additionally synchronises with all blocking streams, so a library call on the default stream silently serialises your carefully overlapped pipeline unless you compile with `--default-stream per-thread` or create streams with `cudaStreamNonBlocking`.

L4.prompt_tpl: Host code does: start host timer, launch kernel, stop host timer, print {t} microseconds for a kernel processing {n} elements. Why is the number wrong?
L4.answer: The launch is asynchronous, so the timer measured only the enqueue. Either synchronise before stopping the timer or use cudaEvent timing on the stream.
L4.explanation: For $2^{26}$ floats a bandwidth-bound kernel cannot finish in microseconds; on A100 at 2039 GB/s a three-array elementwise pass over $2^{26}$ elements needs at least 395 microseconds. A 12 microsecond reading is measuring the driver, not the GPU.

L4.prompt_tpl: You created {n} non-default streams and see zero overlap in Nsight Systems. Name the two most likely causes.
L4.answer: Something is running on the legacy default stream, which implicitly synchronises with all blocking streams; or the copies use pageable host memory, which the driver stages synchronously.
L4.explanation: Create streams with cudaStreamNonBlocking or compile with --default-stream per-thread, and allocate host buffers with cudaHostAlloc. Both are invisible in the source and obvious in a Nsight Systems timeline.

sections.t: Moving data: host, device, and the async copy path
sections.note: Every byte you do not move is the cheapest optimisation available.

L0.cloze: Host buffers must be {{c1::pinned}} (via `cudaMallocHost` or `cudaHostAlloc`) for `cudaMemcpyAsync` to actually be {{c2::asynchronous}}; pageable memory is {{c3::staged}} through a driver bounce buffer.

concepts.L1: The DMA engine can only read host pages that cannot be swapped out. Pinned memory is page-locked at allocation, so the copy engine reads it directly. Pageable memory is copied by the driver into a pinned staging buffer first, on the calling thread.
concepts.L2: `cudaMemcpyAsync` on pageable memory is silently synchronous, and this is the reason most first attempts at copy-compute overlap show no overlap at all. The call still returns a success code; nothing in the API tells you the DMA path was not used.
concepts.L3: Pinning is a global resource: page-locked pages cannot be reclaimed by the OS, so over-pinning degrades the whole machine, and `cudaMallocHost` is slow enough that you allocate once and reuse. The ceiling is PCIe-bound: a Gen4 x16 link tops out near 32 GB/s per direction, and pageable transfers land well under that because of the extra host-side memcpy. Write-combined pinned memory raises host-to-device throughput by bypassing L2 snooping but makes host reads of that buffer catastrophically slow, so use it only for write-once staging. Measure the achieved rate with the CUDA samples `bandwidthTest`; it depends on the link, the chipset and the NUMA node.

L4.prompt_tpl: A pipeline uses {n} streams, cudaMemcpyAsync and malloc'd host buffers, and Nsight Systems shows the copies serialised with the kernels. What is the fix?
L4.answer: Allocate the host buffers with cudaMallocHost or cudaHostAlloc. Pageable source memory forces the driver to stage the copy synchronously, so nothing overlaps.
L4.explanation: The DMA engine requires page-locked memory. Without it the driver does a host-side memcpy into its own pinned buffer on the calling thread, which blocks and defeats the stream structure entirely. The API returns success either way.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why would you allocate {mb} MB of write-combined pinned memory for uploads but never for downloads?
L4.answer: Write-combined memory is uncached on the host, so CPU writes stream out efficiently but CPU reads are extremely slow. Uploads only write; downloads are read back by the host.
L4.explanation: cudaHostAllocWriteCombined skips CPU cache allocation and L2 snooping, which helps host-to-device DMA. Any host read of that buffer bypasses the cache and pays full memory latency per access, so a download buffer must be ordinary pinned memory.

L0.cloze: Split the work into {{c1::chunks}}, issue copy-kernel-copy per chunk into a rotating set of {{c2::streams}}, so chunk k's compute overlaps chunk k+1's {{c3::transfer}}.

concepts.L1: Chunking turns a serial copy-compute-copy into a pipeline. With enough chunks the total time approaches the maximum of the three stages rather than their sum, bounded by the number of copy engines the device has in each direction.
concepts.L2: More streams do not help past the number of copy engines. Most datacentre parts have two DMA engines, one per direction, so beyond about three streams you are only adding launch overhead. The win comes from chunk count, not stream count.
concepts.L3: Model it as a three-stage pipeline with per-chunk times $t_{H}$, $t_{K}$, $t_{D}$ and $n$ chunks. Serial time is $n(t_{H}+t_{K}+t_{D})$. Pipelined time is roughly $(t_{H}+t_{K}+t_{D}) + (n-1)\max(t_{H}, t_{K}, t_{D})$: one full latency to fill the pipe, then one stage time per chunk. With $t_{H}=t_{K}=t_{D}=t$ and $n=8$ that is $3t + 7t = 10t$ against $24t$, a 2.4 times speedup, converging to 3 times as $n$ grows. Chunks that are too small stop amortising launch overhead, typically a few microseconds each; chunks that are too large leave the pipe empty at the ends. Confirm the overlap in a Nsight Systems timeline, never by arithmetic alone.

L4.prompt_tpl: Per-chunk upload, kernel and download each take {t} ms. With {n} chunks and enough streams, give serial time, pipelined time and the speedup. Answer with the pipelined time in milliseconds.
L4.answer: serial = 3*n*t; pipelined = 3t + (n-1)t = (n+2)t; speedup = 3n/(n+2). For t=1,n=8: 24 ms, 10 ms, 2.4x.
L4.explanation: Fill the pipe once at cost $3t$, then retire one chunk per $t$. Checks: (t=1,n=8) gives 24, 10, 2.4x; (t=2,n=16) gives 96, 36, 2.67x; (t=5,n=4) gives 60, 30, 2.0x. The limit as $n \to \infty$ is 3 times, never more, because there are three equal stages.

L4.prompt_tpl: You already use {n} streams and see full overlap. Would going to {m} streams help?
options: Yes, more streams always mean more concurrency
No, the copy engines are already saturated; add chunks instead if the pipe is not full
No, CUDA supports at most 4 streams
L4.answer: No, the copy engines are already saturated; add chunks instead if the pipe is not full
L4.explanation: Concurrency is limited by hardware copy engines (typically one per direction) and by SM capacity, not by the number of stream handles. CUDA imposes no small cap on streams; extra ones cost launch bookkeeping and nothing else.

concepts.t: Unified memory and when it hurts

L0.cloze: `{{c1::cudaMallocManaged}}` gives one pointer valid on both sides; pages migrate on {{c2::fault}}, and `{{c3::cudaMemPrefetchAsync}}` moves them before the fault happens.

concepts.L1: Unified memory gives a single address valid on host and device. On Pascal and later the driver migrates 4 KB-granularity pages on demand via GPU page faults, and can oversubscribe device memory by evicting pages back to the host.
concepts.L2: The convenience is real and the default performance is often terrible, because a fault-driven migration costs far more than a bulk copy of the same bytes. A kernel that strides through a large managed array can fault on nearly every page, turning a bandwidth-bound loop into a sequence of round trips through the driver.
concepts.L3: Demand paging replaces one large DMA with many small ones plus a fault-handling round trip each. Migrating 1 GB as a single `cudaMemcpy` over PCIe Gen4 at roughly 25 GB/s is about 40 ms; migrating the same gigabyte as 262144 separate 4 KB fault-driven transfers pays per-fault driver and TLB cost on top of the same bytes, and is routinely an order of magnitude worse. `cudaMemPrefetchAsync` recovers most of the gap by issuing the bulk move ahead of the kernel, and `cudaMemAdvise` with `SetReadMostly` replicates read-only data so both sides get a local copy. Unified memory wins on oversubscription and pointer-rich structures; it loses on a hot loop over a large array you could have prefetched.

L4.prompt_tpl: You migrate {gb} GB over a link that sustains {bw} GB/s. Give the ideal bulk-copy time, and say how many 4 KB page faults a fully demand-paged migration would take. Answer with the ideal bulk-copy time in seconds.
L4.answer: time = gb/bw seconds; faults = gb*2^30/4096. For 1 GB at 25 GB/s: 40 ms and 262144 faults.
L4.explanation: Checks: 1 GB at 25 GB/s is 0.040 s with 262144 faults; 4 GB at 50 GB/s is 0.080 s with 1048576 faults. The bytes are identical; the difference is per-fault driver work, so the fix is to prefetch rather than to change the allocation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your managed-memory kernel over {mb} MB is {x} times slower than the explicit-copy version. What do you try first?
L4.answer: cudaMemPrefetchAsync the range to the device on the kernel's stream before launch, and cudaMemAdvise read-mostly data. Then re-measure.
L4.explanation: The gap is almost always fault-driven migration, not the allocator. Prefetch converts thousands of small fault transfers into one bulk DMA and usually recovers most of the difference. Nsight Systems shows the faults directly on the Unified Memory row.

concepts.t: cp.async: copying global to shared without the register file

L0.cloze: `cp.async` copies {{c1::global}} to {{c2::shared}} without passing through registers; you `commit_group` then `{{c3::wait_group}}` to control how many copies stay in flight.

concepts.L1: Before Ampere, staging global data into shared memory meant a global load into a register, then a shared store, so the register file and the issue slots were on the critical path. `cp.async` issues a direct DRAM-to-SRAM copy the SM tracks asynchronously.
concepts.L2: `cp.async` is not free asynchrony: it only helps if you have real work to put between the issue and the wait. Issuing a group and immediately waiting on it is slower than an ordinary load, because you have added tracking overhead and removed the load-use scheduling the compiler would have done.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is what makes multi-stage software pipelining practical. With $k$ stages of shared-memory buffer you issue the copy for tile $i+k-1$, then compute on tile $i$, then `cp.async.wait_group k-2` before consuming the next. Registers stay free for the accumulator tile instead of being burned on staging, which is exactly the pressure that limits register-tiled GEMM. The `.cg` qualifier bypasses L1 and caches in L2 only, appropriate for data you will read once; `.ca` caches in both. Sizes are 4, 8 or 16 bytes per instruction and the 16-byte form additionally requires 16-byte alignment. In Triton this is what `num_stages` compiles into; in CUTLASS it is the `Stages` template parameter.

L4.prompt_tpl: A GEMM uses {k} shared-memory stages with cp.async. Explain what wait_group argument the inner loop should use and why.
L4.answer: wait_group k-2, so that k-1 groups have been issued and all but the one you are about to consume may still be in flight. With k stages you keep k-1 copies outstanding.
L4.explanation: The pipeline holds one buffer being computed on and k-1 being filled. Waiting for zero outstanding groups collapses the pipeline to a synchronous copy; waiting for too many lets you read a buffer whose copy has not landed. This is the same depth parameter Triton exposes as num_stages.

L4.prompt_tpl: Adding cp.async to a kernel with {n} independent tiles made it {x} percent slower. Most likely cause?
options: cp.async is slower than ld.global on Ampere
There is not enough independent work between issue and wait, so you pay tracking cost for no overlap
The data was not 16-byte aligned so the copy silently failed
L4.answer: There is not enough independent work between issue and wait, so you pay tracking cost for no overlap
L4.explanation: Asynchrony pays only when something useful fills the latency. With one or two tiles there is no next tile to prefetch, so the commit and wait are pure overhead. Misalignment would fault or fall back, not cost a few percent.

concepts.t: TMA: the Hopper tensor memory accelerator

L0.cloze: TMA copies a whole multidimensional {{c1::tile}} described by a `{{c2::tensor map}}` built on the host, issued by a {{c3::single}} thread and completed against an mbarrier.

concepts.L1: TMA is a dedicated copy unit introduced on Hopper (sm_90). One thread issues a descriptor-driven copy of an entire multidimensional tile between global and shared memory; the unit computes all the addresses, handles out-of-bounds padding, and signals completion on an mbarrier.
concepts.L2: The saving is not bandwidth, it is address arithmetic and issue slots. With `cp.async` every lane computes its own address and issues its own instruction; with TMA one thread issues once, so the other 31 lanes and all their index math disappear from the instruction stream, which is what frees a warp to be a pure producer.
concepts.L3: Consider staging a 128 by 64 bf16 tile. With `cp.async` at 16 bytes per instruction that is $128 \times 64 \times 2 / 16 = 1024$ copy instructions plus the index arithmetic to compute 1024 addresses, spread across the block. With TMA it is one instruction against a descriptor that already encodes shape, strides, box size and swizzle. Out-of-bounds boxes are filled with zeros by the hardware, which removes the boundary-condition branches that clutter a hand-written tiled loop. The descriptor is 128 bytes, 64-byte aligned, and built on the host with `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled`. TMA plus mbarrier plus warp specialisation is the structural core of FlashAttention-3 and Hopper CUTLASS.

L4.prompt_tpl: Staging a {M} by {N} bf16 tile into shared memory. How many 16-byte cp.async instructions does that take, versus TMA? Answer with the number of cp.async instructions.
L4.answer: cp.async: M*N*2/16 instructions. TMA: 1. For 128 by 64: 1024 versus 1.
L4.explanation: Checks: 128 by 64 bf16 is 16384 bytes, so 1024 sixteen-byte copies; 64 by 128 is the same 1024; 128 by 128 would be 2048. TMA issues once against a descriptor, so the instruction count and all the per-lane address arithmetic vanish from the SM.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does TMA make warp specialisation with {p} producer warps practical, when cp.async did not?
L4.answer: Because a single thread can issue an entire tile copy, one small producer warp can keep the buffers full without spending issue slots on per-lane addressing, leaving the rest of the block free for the math pipes.
L4.explanation: With cp.async the copy work is spread over all lanes, so a dedicated producer warp could only move 1/N of the tile per issue. TMA collapses the copy to one instruction plus an mbarrier arrival, which is what FlashAttention-3 and Hopper CUTLASS exploit.

sections.t: Memory access rules, with the address arithmetic worked out
sections.note: Coalescing and bank conflicts are arithmetic, not folklore. Compute them before you profile.

L0.cloze: The memory system fetches in {{c1::32}}-byte sectors; an aligned warp-wide float load spans {{c2::128}} bytes and therefore {{c3::4}} sectors, the minimum possible.

concepts.L1: The L1 and L2 caches move data in 32-byte sectors, four to a 128-byte line. A warp's 32 lane addresses are coalesced into the set of distinct sectors they touch. Efficiency is useful bytes over sectors fetched times 32.
concepts.L2: Coalescing is about the set of sectors, not about the order of the lanes. A warp whose 32 lanes read the same 128-byte region in shuffled order is perfectly coalesced; a warp reading 32 addresses in ascending order but four bytes apart from a misaligned base touches five sectors, not four.
concepts.L3: Work the cases for 32 lanes reading floats. Aligned unit stride: addresses span bytes $[0, 128)$, sectors $\lfloor a/32 \rfloor \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, so 4 sectors, 128 bytes moved for 128 useful, 100 percent. Base offset by one float: span is $[4, 132)$, sectors $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, so 5 sectors, 160 bytes for 128 useful, 80 percent. Stride 2 floats: span $[0, 256)$ hitting every sector, 8 sectors, 256 bytes for 128, 50 percent. Stride 32 floats, which is a column of a row-major matrix: no two lanes share a sector, 32 sectors, 1024 bytes for 128 useful, 12.5 percent. That last case is the eightfold penalty behind every naive transpose and every row-versus-column indexing bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: A warp of 32 lanes reads floats with stride {s} elements from an aligned base. How many 32-byte sectors are touched, and what is the bytes-delivered efficiency? Answer with the number of sectors touched.
L4.answer: sectors = min(32, max(4, 4*s)); efficiency = 128/(32*sectors). s=1: 4 sectors, 100 percent. s=2: 8, 50. s=4: 16, 25. s=8: 32, 12.5.
L4.explanation: With stride $s$ floats the warp spans $128s$ bytes; the sectors touched are $\min(32, 4s)$ once $s \geq 1$, saturating at 32 because there are only 32 lanes. Beyond $s = 8$ every lane already owns a sector, so the efficiency floor is 12.5 percent.

L4.prompt_tpl: The base pointer of a float array is offset by {k} floats from a 128-byte boundary. How many sectors does one warp-wide unit-stride read touch? Answer with the number of sectors.
L4.answer: 5 sectors for k not a multiple of 8; 4 sectors when 4k is a multiple of 32, i.e. k divisible by 8.
L4.explanation: The read spans bytes $[4k, 4k+128)$. If $4k \bmod 32 = 0$ that is exactly 4 sectors; otherwise it straddles and touches 5, costing 25 percent extra traffic. Checks: k=1 gives 5, k=4 gives 5, k=8 gives 4, k=0 gives 4.

concepts.t: Vectorised access: float4 and the alignment contract

L0.cloze: A `float4` load compiles to a single {{c1::128}}-bit instruction and requires {{c2::16}}-byte alignment; `cudaMalloc` guarantees at least {{c3::256}}-byte alignment of the base.

concepts.L1: One 128-bit load moves the same bytes as four 32-bit loads with a quarter of the instructions and a quarter of the memory-pipe requests. On bandwidth-bound kernels with low occupancy this is often the difference between 70 and 95 percent of peak.
concepts.L2: Vectorising does not reduce bytes moved, so it cannot help a kernel that is already saturating DRAM with enough warps in flight. It helps by cutting issued requests, which matters when you are request-limited or issue-limited, and it silently breaks correctness the moment the pointer is not 16-byte aligned.
concepts.L3: A warp of 32 lanes doing `float4` loads spans $32 \times 16 = 512$ bytes, which is 16 sectors, and delivers 512 useful bytes: still 100 percent efficient, but the warp now covers four times as much data per instruction. The instruction count for a length-$n$ copy drops from $n$ to $n/4$ loads and stores. The alignment contract is unforgiving: `cudaMalloc` returns 256-byte-aligned memory so `reinterpret_cast<float4*>(base)` is safe, but any offset that is not a multiple of four floats is not, and the failure mode is a misaligned-address fault or, worse, silently wrong data on some paths. Handle a tail of $n \bmod 4$ elements with a scalar epilogue rather than by giving up on the vector path.

L4.prompt_tpl: Copying {n} floats. How many load instructions does the scalar version issue per warp-load, versus the float4 version, and how many tail elements need a scalar epilogue? Answer with the number of float4 vector loads.
L4.answer: scalar: n loads; float4: floor(n/4) vector loads plus n mod 4 scalar. n=1000003 gives 250000 vector loads and 3 tail elements.
L4.explanation: Checks: n=1000003 gives 250000 and tail 3; n=65536 gives 16384 and tail 0; n=1048575 gives 262143 and tail 3. Bytes moved are identical in all cases; only the instruction and request count changes, which is why this helps issue-limited kernels and not DRAM-saturated ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel does `reinterpret_cast<const float4*>(x + {k})[i]` where x came from cudaMalloc. When is this wrong?
L4.answer: Whenever k is not a multiple of 4. x is 256-byte aligned, so x+k is 16-byte aligned only if 4k is a multiple of 16.
L4.explanation: float4 requires 16-byte alignment. x+1 is 4 bytes past a 256-byte boundary and the cast is undefined behaviour; in practice you get a misaligned address fault. Offsets of 4, 8 or 12 floats are fine; 1, 2 and 3 are not.

concepts.t: Shared memory banks: computing the conflict

L0.cloze: Shared memory has {{c1::32}} banks of 4-byte words; the bank of word address a is `a % {{c2::32}}`, so a column of a `[32][32]` tile puts all lanes in {{c3::one}} bank.

concepts.L1: Shared memory is 32 banks wide, each serving one 4-byte word per cycle. A warp access is split into as many cycles as the largest number of distinct addresses any single bank must serve. Same-address reads broadcast for free; different addresses in one bank serialise.
concepts.L2: Broadcast is not a conflict. All 32 lanes reading the identical address is one cycle, not 32, because the bank broadcasts. The conflict condition is distinct words mapping to the same bank, which is why `tile[ty][tx]` is fine and `tile[tx][ty]` is a 32-way disaster on a 32-wide tile.
concepts.L3: Bank index is $b(a) = a \bmod 32$ for word address $a$. For `__shared__ float tile[32][32]`, element $(r, c)$ has $a = 32r + c$, so $b = c \bmod 32 = c$. A row access ($c = $ lane) gives 32 distinct banks: one cycle. A column access ($r = $ lane) gives $b = c$ for all 32 lanes at 32 distinct addresses: 32 cycles. Pad the row to 33: $a = 33r + c$, so $b = (33r + c) \bmod 32 = (r + c) \bmod 32$, and a column access with $r$ ranging over $0..31$ yields 32 distinct banks: back to one cycle, at a cost of $32 \times 4 = 128$ extra bytes of shared memory. Note that with 8-byte or 16-byte accesses the hardware splits the warp into phases first, so the analysis is per phase.

L4.prompt_tpl: For `__shared__ float t[32][{W}]`, a warp reads t[lane][{c}]. How many distinct banks are touched and what is the conflict degree?
L4.answer: bank(lane) = (W*lane + c) mod 32; degree = 32/#distinct. W=32: 1 bank, 32-way. W=33: 32 banks, conflict-free. W=34: 16 banks, 2-way. W=16: 2 banks, 16-way.
L4.explanation: The number of distinct values of $W \cdot \mathrm{lane} \bmod 32$ over 32 lanes is $32/\gcd(W, 32)$. Odd $W$ gives $\gcd = 1$ and no conflict; $W = 34$ gives $\gcd = 2$ and a 2-way conflict; $W = 32$ gives $\gcd = 32$ and the worst case.

L4.prompt_tpl: All {n} lanes of a warp read the same shared-memory address. How many cycles does the access take?
options: 32, because 32 lanes hit one bank
1, because identical addresses are broadcast
2, one for the read and one for the broadcast
L4.answer: 1, because identical addresses are broadcast
L4.explanation: A bank conflict requires distinct word addresses in the same bank. Identical addresses are served by a single broadcast, which is why lookup tables and shared scalars in shared memory are cheap. This is the most commonly mis-stated rule in the model.

L0.cloze: Padding to a stride coprime with 32 costs {{c1::extra memory}}; an {{c2::XOR}} swizzle permutes the index instead and keeps the footprint {{c3::unchanged}}.

concepts.L1: Two ways to break bank conflicts. Padding changes the row stride so the bank function stops being constant down a column. Swizzling permutes the within-row index with an XOR so that each row is stored under a different rotation.
concepts.L2: Padding is free in effort and expensive in the one place it hurts: it breaks the 16-byte alignment that `ldmatrix` and the tensor-core fragment loads require, and it wastes shared memory that occupancy is measured in. Every tensor-core kernel swizzles instead; padding is a scalar-kernel technique.
concepts.L3: With padding, stride $W = 33$ gives $b = (33r + c) \bmod 32 = (r + c) \bmod 32$: a column becomes a full residue system, conflict-free. Cost is $32 \times 4 = 128$ bytes per tile and the loss of the property that a row is 128-byte aligned. With an XOR swizzle, element $(r, c)$ lives at $32r + (c \oplus (r \bmod 32))$, so the bank is $(c \oplus (r \bmod 32)) \bmod 32$; for fixed $c$ and $r$ ranging over $0..31$ the XOR is a bijection, so again all 32 banks appear exactly once. The footprint is unchanged and 16-byte chunks stay aligned when the swizzle acts on whole chunks, which is why CuTe parameterises `Swizzle<B,M,S>` by chunk size.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that storing element (r, c) at offset {W}*r + (c XOR (r mod 32)) is conflict-free for a column read with fixed c and r = 0..31.
L4.answer: Bank is (c XOR (r mod 32)) mod 32. For fixed c, r -> c XOR r is a bijection on the 32 residues, so the 32 lanes cover all 32 banks exactly once.
L4.explanation: XOR with a fixed value is an involution and therefore a permutation of the 5-bit index space. Since W = 32 contributes a multiple of 32 to the address, it vanishes modulo 32, leaving the XOR term to spread the lanes across all banks.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tensor-core GEMM stages a {M} by {K} bf16 tile in shared memory. Padding or swizzle?
L4.answer: Swizzle. ldmatrix and the mma fragment loads require 16-byte-aligned, contiguously addressable chunks; padding breaks that alignment and also spends shared memory that limits occupancy.
L4.explanation: Padding is the right answer for a scalar transpose or reduction where accesses are single words. For tensor-core paths the fragment loaders read 16-byte groups at fixed offsets, so the layout must stay dense; CUTLASS and Triton both emit XOR swizzles here.

L0.cloze: `-Xptxas -v` prints registers used and `{{c1::spill}}` stores; `__launch_bounds__(T, B)` asks for {{c2::B}} resident blocks and caps registers at `{{c3::65536}}/(T*B)`.

concepts.L1: Each SM has a fixed register file, 65536 32-bit registers on every architecture from Volta through Hopper. Registers per thread times threads per block times resident blocks must fit. When the compiler cannot fit, it spills to local memory, which is DRAM.
concepts.L2: A spill in the inner loop is far worse than the occupancy you were protecting. Going from 64 to 32 registers per thread doubles occupancy on paper and can halve throughput, because the accumulator tile that used to live in registers now round-trips to global memory on every iteration.
concepts.L3: On a 65536-register SM with 256-thread blocks: 64 registers per thread gives $256 \times 64 = 16384$ per block, so 4 blocks, 32 warps, 50 percent occupancy. 32 registers gives 8 blocks, 64 warps, 100 percent. But an 8 by 8 register tile in a GEMM needs 64 accumulators alone, before any addressing or staging values, so forcing 32 registers guarantees spills. `__launch_bounds__(T, B)` states the trade: ptxas allocates at most $65536/(T \cdot B)$ registers per thread and spills if the code needs more. Read the spill counters, not occupancy: zero spills at 50 percent beats 40 spill stores at 100 percent.

L4.prompt_tpl: __launch_bounds__({T}, {B}) on an SM with 65536 registers. What register cap does ptxas apply per thread? Answer with the register cap per thread.
L4.answer: cap = 65536 / (T*B), rounded down to the allocation granularity. (256,4) gives 64; (128,8) gives 64; (512,2) gives 64; (256,8) gives 32.
L4.explanation: The product of block size, resident blocks and registers per thread cannot exceed the register file. Checks: (256,4) and (128,8) and (512,2) all give 64 registers; asking for (256,8) halves it to 32, which is where a register-tiled kernel starts spilling.

L4.prompt_tpl: Raising the thread tile from 4 by 4 to {a} by {a} made the GEMM {x} percent slower. ptxas reports nonzero spill stores. Diagnose.
L4.answer: The accumulator tile no longer fits in registers, so the innermost loop spills to local memory, which is global DRAM. Shrink the tile, or raise the register cap and accept lower occupancy.
L4.explanation: An a by a thread tile needs at least a*a accumulator registers plus staging: 64 for 8 by 8 and 256 for 16 by 16, the latter exceeding the 255-register per-thread hardware limit outright. Spill traffic in the inner loop swamps any tiling gain.

prereqs: Choosing a launch configuration: occupancy arithmetic in practice

L0.cloze: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs divided by {{c1::DRAM bytes moved}}; the ridge point is peak FLOP/s divided by peak {{c2::bandwidth}}, and a kernel below it is {{c3::memory}} bound.

concepts.L1: Every kernel sits somewhere on a line: achievable FLOP/s equals the minimum of peak compute and arithmetic intensity times peak bandwidth. Which side of the ridge you are on decides whether more math or less traffic is the optimisation.
concepts.L2: The ridge point moves with the datatype and rises every generation, which is the memory wall as a number. A100's FP32 ridge is 9.6 FLOP/byte, its BF16 tensor ridge 153, a TPU v7's 626 at FP8: a kernel compute-bound on one part is memory-bound on the next without changing, which is why fusion became mandatory, not optional.
concepts.L3: Compute the two numbers from datasheets and divide. A100 80GB SXM: 19.5 TFLOP/s FP32 over 2039 GB/s is 9.56 FLOP/byte, or 153.0 with 312 TFLOP/s BF16 tensor; H100 SXM is 20.0 FP32 and 295.3 BF16; TPU v7 Ironwood is 4614 TFLOP/s FP8 over 7.37 TB/s of HBM, a ridge of 626. Now place kernels. SAXPY moves 12 bytes for 2 FLOP: AI $= 0.167$, hopelessly memory bound. A 4096-cube FP32 GEMM does $2N^{3} = 137.4$ GFLOP over at least $12N^{2} = 201$ MB: AI $= 683$, compute bound only if tiling actually achieves that minimum, while the naive version moves 550 GB and sits at $0.25$. Batch-1 LLM decode reads each weight for one MAC: 2 FLOP/byte, 0.32 percent of an Ironwood.

L4.prompt_tpl: An elementwise kernel reads {r} float arrays and writes {w}, doing {f} FLOP per element. Give its arithmetic intensity and say which side of the A100 FP32 ridge (9.56 FLOP/byte) it lands on. Answer with the arithmetic intensity.
L4.answer: AI = f / (4*(r+w)). (2,1,1) gives 0.0833; (3,2,8) gives 0.4; (1,1,20) gives 2.5. All are below 9.56, so all are memory bound.
L4.explanation: Each float touched costs 4 bytes of DRAM traffic in the no-reuse case. Even 20 FLOP per element on one input and one output is only 2.5 FLOP/byte, still under the ridge, which is why almost every pointwise neural-network op is bandwidth bound and why fusion is the only lever.

L4.prompt_tpl: A square GEMM of size N = {N} in FP32. Give total FLOPs, the minimum DRAM traffic, and the resulting arithmetic intensity. Answer with the arithmetic intensity.
L4.answer: FLOPs = 2N^3; min bytes = 12N^2; AI = N/6. N=4096: 137.44 GFLOP, 201.3 MB, AI = 682.7.
L4.explanation: Reading A and B once and writing C once is $3N^{2}$ floats, or $12N^{2}$ bytes. Checks: N=1024 gives 2.147 GFLOP, 12.58 MB, AI 170.7; N=8192 gives 1099.5 GFLOP, 805.3 MB, AI 1365.3. AI grows linearly with N, which is why small GEMMs are memory bound and large ones are not.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the arithmetic intensity of batch-{b} LLM decoding, where each weight is read once from memory and used in one multiply-accumulate, and express the achievable fraction of peak against a ridge point of {r} FLOP per byte.
L4.answer: At batch 1 with 1-byte weights, each byte supports one multiply-add, so intensity is 2 FLOP per byte. Achievable fraction $= 2/r$. Against a ridge of 626 that is 0.32 percent. At batch $b$ each weight is reused $b$ times, giving intensity $2b$ and fraction $2b/r$.
L4.explanation: The linear dependence on batch size is the entire economic argument for batched serving: intensity, and therefore utilisation, is proportional to batch. It also explains why a decode-optimised part should trade peak FLOPs for bandwidth, which is why inference and training silicon are diverging.

sections.note: The sync primitives are where correctness bugs live and where the fastest reductions come from.

L0.cloze: `__syncthreads()` is a {{c1::block}}-wide barrier plus a memory fence; every thread of the block must reach the {{c2::same}} barrier, and you need a second one before {{c3::overwriting}} shared data others still read.

concepts.L1: `__syncthreads()` blocks until every thread in the block arrives and makes all prior shared and global writes by those threads visible to the rest. It is a barrier and a fence at once; without the fence half the point would be missing.
concepts.L2: One barrier is almost never enough. The classic bug is a single `__syncthreads()` after filling shared memory but none before refilling it on the next loop iteration, so fast warps overwrite tiles that slow warps are still reading. The kernel produces correct results on small inputs and garbage under load.
concepts.L3: A tiled loop needs two barriers per iteration: one after the shared-memory store so all threads can read the tile, and one after the compute so no thread starts the next store while another is still reading. Omitting the second creates a write-after-read race that the hardware will not diagnose. The barrier must be reached by all threads: a `__syncthreads()` inside a divergent branch is undefined behaviour and on some architectures hangs the block. The barrier is per block: it says nothing about other blocks. Warp-level code needs `__syncwarp()`, because from Volta independent thread scheduling means lanes are not implicitly in step.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tiled GEMM loops over {k} K-tiles with exactly one __syncthreads() per iteration, placed after the shared-memory stores. What breaks and when?
L4.answer: A write-after-read race: a fast warp begins storing tile i+1 while a slow warp still reads tile i. It needs a second barrier after the compute loop.
L4.explanation: Warps within a block do not run in lockstep. The failure is data-dependent and load-dependent, so it usually passes on small matrices and fails at production tile counts, which makes it one of the hardest CUDA bugs to reproduce. compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck finds it.

L4.prompt_tpl: What is the behaviour of `if (threadIdx.x < {n}) {{ __syncthreads(); }}` in a {T}-thread block?
L4.answer: Undefined behaviour. The barrier must be reached by all threads of the block; in practice it can hang the block or silently release early.
L4.explanation: CUDA specifies that __syncthreads() is only defined when every thread in the block executes it, and executes the same one. Compilers do not diagnose the divergent case, and the observed behaviour varies by architecture, which is why it is a correctness rule rather than a performance rule.

prereqs: The memory hierarchy you can address

L0.cloze: A divergent branch makes the warp execute {{c1::both}} sides serially with lanes {{c2::masked}}; branching on `i >> 5` keeps whole {{c3::warps}} together and costs nothing.

concepts.L1: Lanes of a warp share issue. When lanes take different sides of a branch the warp executes each side in turn with the non-participating lanes predicated off, so the cost is the sum of the paths, not the maximum or the average.
concepts.L2: Divergence is only a problem within a warp: `if (blockIdx.x % 2)` is free, `if (threadIdx.x % 2)` doubles the body. And since Volta each thread has its own program counter, so diverged lanes may never reconverge on their own and lockstep idioms need an explicit `__syncwarp()`.
concepts.L3: Cost model: for a two-way branch with bodies of $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ cycles, a converged warp pays $\max$ over nothing at all, it pays one body; a diverged warp pays $c_{1} + c_{2}$. With an $n$-way switch fully diverged across 32 lanes you pay the sum of all $n$ bodies, and a data-dependent `while` loop pays the longest trip count for every lane. This is why bucketing data so a warp's lanes take the same path can beat any memory optimisation. Independent thread scheduling changes semantics, not cost: reconvergence at the immediate post-dominator is no longer guaranteed, so code that assumed lanes had exchanged data on falling out of a branch needs `__syncwarp()`.

L4.prompt_tpl: A warp hits a {n}-way switch, fully diverged across its lanes, where each case body costs {c} cycles. What does the warp pay, and what would it pay if all 32 lanes took the same case? Answer with the diverged cost in cycles.
L4.answer: Diverged: n*c cycles. Converged: c cycles. n=4, c=10 gives 40 versus 10.
L4.explanation: Each distinct path taken by at least one lane is issued once for the whole warp with the others masked. Checks: (4,10) is 40 versus 10; (8,25) is 200 versus 25; (2,10) is 20 versus 10. The slowdown factor equals the number of distinct paths present in the warp, capped at 32.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which branch condition costs nothing in divergence terms for a block of {T} threads?
options: if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0)
if ((threadIdx.x / 32) % 2 == 0)
if (data[threadIdx.x] > 0)
L4.answer: if ((threadIdx.x / 32) % 2 == 0)
L4.explanation: Dividing by 32 makes the predicate constant across each warp, so every warp takes exactly one side and nothing is masked. The modulo-2 lane test splits every warp 16-16, and the data-dependent test splits unpredictably.

prereqs: Warps: the unit that actually executes

L0.cloze: `__shfl_down_sync({{c1::mask}}, var, delta)` moves a register from lane `i+delta` to lane `i` with no {{c2::shared memory}} and no barrier; the mask names the {{c3::participating}} lanes.

concepts.L1: Shuffle instructions read another lane's register directly through the register file crossbar. They need no shared memory, no barrier, and no address arithmetic, and they are the reason a warp-level reduction is five instructions rather than a shared-memory tree.
concepts.L2: The mask is not optional decoration and it is not the set of lanes you wish were active. It must name exactly the lanes that will execute the instruction; passing `0xffffffff` inside a divergent branch is undefined behaviour, and the non-`_sync` variants were removed in CUDA 9 precisely because people got this wrong.
concepts.L3: A full warp reduction is $\log_{2} 32 = 5$ shuffle-and-add steps with deltas 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; after them lane 0 holds the sum. Compare the shared-memory tree: 5 rounds of store, barrier, load, add, with a shared array and bank-conflict risk at each level. The butterfly form `__shfl_xor_sync(mask, v, 1 << k)` for $k = 0..4$ leaves the result in every lane instead of only lane 0, at the same instruction count, which is what you want when all lanes need the total. Shuffles operate on 32-bit registers, so a `double` costs two of them and the compiler emits the pair for you. All of this is why the last stage of a fast reduction abandons shared memory entirely once the live data fits in one warp.

L4.prompt_tpl: A warp-wide sum via __shfl_down_sync with {n} lanes. How many shuffle-add steps, and what deltas? Answer with the number of shuffle-add steps.
L4.answer: log2(n) steps. n=32: 5 steps with deltas 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. n=16: 4 steps, deltas 8,4,2,1. n=8: 3 steps, deltas 4,2,1.
L4.explanation: Each step halves the number of lanes holding partial sums, so the count is $\log_{2} n$ and the deltas are the descending powers of two starting at $n/2$. The result ends in lane 0; use the XOR butterfly instead if every lane needs it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Inside `if (tid < {n})` a kernel calls `__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 16)`. What is wrong?
L4.answer: The mask claims all 32 lanes participate, but the branch has masked some off. The mask must match the actually-active lanes; use __activemask() or restructure so the whole warp participates.
L4.explanation: A _sync primitive requires that every lane named in the mask reaches that instruction. Naming absent lanes is undefined behaviour and in practice returns garbage or hangs. The usual fix is to give inactive lanes an identity value and let the whole warp run the reduction.

L0.cloze: `__ballot_sync` returns a {{c1::32-bit mask}} of predicates; `__popc(m & ((1<<lane)-1))` gives each lane its {{c2::rank}}, so a warp can do one {{c3::atomic}} instead of 32.

concepts.L1: Vote functions collapse a per-lane predicate into a warp-wide value: `__ballot_sync` returns the bitmask, `__all_sync` and `__any_sync` the reductions. With `__popc` they turn a warp into a tiny prefix-sum machine.
concepts.L2: Warp aggregation is the highest-leverage atomic optimisation and it is invisible in the source. Thirty-two lanes each doing `atomicAdd(counter, 1)` on one address serialise into 32 round trips through L2; electing a leader to add 32 at once is one round trip.
concepts.L3: The idiom is an exclusive prefix sum over one bit per lane, computed by bit tricks. `__ballot_sync` gives mask $m$; `__popc(m)` is the count $n$; `__popc(m \,\&\, ((1 \ll \mathrm{lane}) - 1))` counts set bits strictly below your lane, which is exactly your rank among participating lanes. The leader performs one `atomicAdd(counter, n)` and broadcasts the returned base with a shuffle, and each lane writes at `base + rank`. For a compaction kernel where half the lanes pass, this cuts atomic traffic about 16 times. `__activemask()` gives the currently converged lanes when you cannot know statically who is present.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a stream-compaction kernel, {p} percent of lanes pass the predicate on average. By what factor does warp aggregation reduce atomic operations on the output counter? Answer with the reduction factor.
L4.answer: From 32*p/100 atomics per warp to 1: a factor of 32p/100. p=50 gives 16x; p=25 gives 8x; p=100 gives 32x.
L4.explanation: Without aggregation each passing lane issues its own atomic to the same address, and same-address atomics serialise at L2. With aggregation the warp issues exactly one regardless of how many lanes passed, so the speedup on that instruction equals the expected number of passing lanes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given ballot mask m and lane id L, derive the expression for this lane's rank among participating lanes, and evaluate it for m = 0x{m} and L = {L}.
L4.answer: rank = __popc(m & ((1u << L) - 1)). For m = 0xF0F0F0F0, L = 5: bits 0..4 of m are 0, so rank 0. For m = 0x0000FFFF, L = 5: bits 0..4 all set, rank 5.
L4.explanation: `(1u << L) - 1` is a mask of the L bits strictly below your lane; ANDing and popcounting gives the exclusive prefix sum of the predicate. This is a two-instruction sequence that replaces a shared-memory scan.

L0.cloze: `cg::tiled_partition<{{c1::32}}>(block)` names a warp as a first-class group; `grid.sync()` needs the kernel launched with `{{c2::cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel}}` and all blocks {{c3::co-resident}}.

concepts.L1: Cooperative groups make the implicit thread hierarchy explicit and typed. A group object carries its size and rank, and algorithms like `cg::reduce` and `cg::inclusive_scan` are written against the group rather than against hard-coded warp masks.
concepts.L2: `grid.sync()` is not a free grid-wide barrier. It requires a cooperative launch, and a cooperative launch requires every block to be simultaneously resident, so your grid size is capped by occupancy times SM count. Exceed it and the launch fails rather than degrading.
concepts.L3: The usable grid for a cooperative launch is at most (resident blocks per SM) times (number of SMs), which you must query with `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` rather than assume. On an A100 with 108 SMs and a kernel achieving 4 resident blocks per SM, that ceiling is 432 blocks; a persistent-kernel design then loops with a grid-stride over the real problem. That is the trade against a second kernel launch, which costs a few microseconds but imposes no residency cap. Groups also fix the mask problem: a `tiled_partition` knows its membership, so `cg::reduce` emits the right mask instead of a hopeful `0xffffffff`.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cooperative kernel achieves {b} resident blocks per SM on a GPU with {sm} SMs. What is the largest legal grid, and how many elements does each block handle for n = {n} with a grid-stride loop? Answer with the largest legal grid in blocks.
L4.answer: max blocks = b*sm; elements per block = ceil(n/(b*sm)). b=4, sm=108 gives 432 blocks and 155345 elements each.
L4.explanation: Checks: (4,108) gives 432 blocks, ceil(67108864/432) = 155345 per block; (2,132) gives 264 blocks; (8,132) gives 1056. Exceeding the residency ceiling makes cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel return an error rather than silently deadlocking, which is the one merciful part of the design.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need a grid-wide barrier {n} times inside one algorithm. Cooperative launch or {n} separate kernel launches?
L4.answer: Few barriers: separate launches, which are simple and impose no grid-size cap. Many barriers in a tight loop: cooperative launch, since a few microseconds of launch overhead per iteration dominates.
L4.explanation: A kernel launch is roughly a few microseconds of overhead and gives unconditional ordering with no residency constraint. grid.sync() is cheaper per barrier but caps the grid at resident blocks times SMs and forces a persistent, grid-stride structure on the whole kernel.

concepts.t: Atomics and what they actually cost

L0.cloze: Global atomics resolve at {{c1::L2}}; shared-memory atomics resolve {{c2::inside the SM}}; float atomicAdd gives non-{{c3::deterministic}} results because the summation order varies.

concepts.L1: An atomic is a read-modify-write performed at a cache level rather than in the SM. Global atomics execute at the L2 slice owning the address, so lanes contending for one address serialise there; shared-memory atomics execute in the SM and are far cheaper.
concepts.L2: Contention, not the atomic instruction, is the cost. Atomics to 4096 distinct addresses run near full throughput because they land on different L2 slices; atomics from every thread to one address are fully serialised. The standard fix is a two-level design: privatise into shared memory, then one atomic per block into global.
concepts.L3: For a 256-bin histogram over $n$ elements with a single global counter array, the naive kernel issues $n$ global atomics with heavy same-address contention. Privatised, each block keeps a 256-bin shared histogram, does $n/\mathrm{blocks}$ cheap shared atomics, then commits 256 global atomics at the end: for $n = 10^{8}$ over 1024 blocks that is 262144 global atomics instead of $10^{8}$, a 381-fold reduction. Add warp aggregation inside the shared phase and the shared traffic drops again. Determinism matters for training: float addition is not associative, so atomic reductions vary in the last bits run to run, which is why deterministic modes replace them with fixed-order trees.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {bins}-bin histogram over n = {n} elements, privatised into shared memory across {blocks} blocks. How many global atomics does the privatised version issue, and what is the reduction factor versus the naive version? Answer with the number of global atomics.
L4.answer: global atomics = bins*blocks; factor = n/(bins*blocks). 256 bins, 1024 blocks: 262144 atomics, 381x fewer.
L4.explanation: Checks: (256,1024) gives 262144 and 381.5x; (1024,1024) gives 1048576 and 95.4x; (256,4096) gives 1048576 and 95.4x. More blocks means more commit traffic, so the privatisation win shrinks as you raise occupancy, which is a real trade rather than a free win.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two runs of the same training step on the same data give losses differing at the {d}th decimal place. The kernel uses atomicAdd on floats. Explain.
L4.answer: Floating-point addition is not associative, and atomics complete in a hardware-determined order that varies run to run, so the partial sums are added in different orders and round differently.
L4.explanation: This is expected behaviour, not a bug. If bitwise reproducibility is required, replace the atomic reduction with a fixed-order tree or use the framework's deterministic algorithms setting, and accept the throughput cost.

sections.note: Every FLOP that matters on a modern GPU goes through one of these. Getting data into the right fragment layout is most of the work.

L0.cloze: A tensor core computes {{c1::D = A*B + C}} on a whole tile in one instruction issued by a {{c2::warp}} (or warpgroup on Hopper), with inputs in low precision and the accumulator in {{c3::fp32}}.

concepts.L1: A tensor core is a matrix-multiply-accumulate unit. One instruction consumes a small tile of A and B held across the registers of a whole warp and accumulates into a tile of C, replacing hundreds of scalar FMAs with one issue.
concepts.L2: The accumulator precision is the point, not a detail. Ampere's `m16n8k16` takes fp16 or bf16 inputs and accumulates in fp32, so a $K$-length dot product does not lose precision the way naive fp16 summation would. Using fp16 accumulation to go faster is exactly how training runs diverge.
concepts.L3: Count the work in one `m16n8k16` instruction: $16 \times 8 \times 16 = 2048$ multiply-accumulates, so $4096$ FLOP, issued once by a 32-lane warp. A scalar FFMA path would need $2048$ instructions across the warp, 64 per lane. That ratio is the whole reason tensor-core peak is an order of magnitude above FP32 peak: A100 is 19.5 TFLOP/s FP32 against 312 TFLOP/s BF16 tensor, a factor of 16. The consequence is that the arithmetic-intensity ridge moves from 9.56 to 153 FLOP/byte on the same chip, so a kernel that fed the FP32 pipes adequately will starve the tensor cores. Feeding them is the whole discipline: `ldmatrix`, swizzled layouts, `cp.async` and TMA all exist to keep this unit busy.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many FLOP does one mma.sync.m{M}n{N}k{K} instruction perform, and how many scalar FFMA instructions would a warp need for the same work? Answer with the FLOP count of one instruction.
L4.answer: FLOP = 2*M*N*K; scalar FFMAs = M*N*K, or M*N*K/32 per lane. m16n8k16: 4096 FLOP, 2048 FFMAs, 64 per lane.
L4.explanation: Each output element accumulates K products, so the tile does $M N K$ multiply-adds, counted as $2 M N K$ FLOP. Checks: m16n8k16 gives 4096 FLOP and 2048 FFMAs; m16n8k8 gives 2048 FLOP and 1024 FFMAs. One issue replaces 64 per-lane instructions.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a GPU with {fp32} TFLOP/s FP32 and {tc} TFLOP/s BF16 tensor over {bw} GB/s, give both ridge points in FLOP/byte. Answer with the tensor-core ridge point.
L4.explanation: A100 80GB SXM: 19.5e12/2039e9 = 9.56 and 312e12/2039e9 = 153.0. H100 SXM: 67e12/3350e9 = 20.0 and 989.4e12/3350e9 = 295.3. Switching to tensor cores multiplies the intensity you must reach by roughly 15, which is why fusion became mandatory.

L0.cloze: A `fragment` is a warp-distributed tile whose per-lane layout is {{c1::opaque}}; `load_matrix_sync` and `mma_sync` must be called by the {{c2::entire warp}}, and the accumulator is typically {{c3::float}}.

concepts.L1: WMMA is the portable C++ face of the tensor cores. A `fragment` is a tile spread across the registers of a warp; the API deliberately hides which lane holds which element, and every operation on a fragment is warp-collective.
concepts.L2: You may not index a fragment. `a.x[i]` exists but the mapping from `i` to a matrix element is unspecified and changes between architectures, so any code that inspects fragment elements is relying on undefined layout. The only defined operations are load, store, fill and multiply-accumulate.
concepts.L3: The opacity is what makes WMMA portable and what makes it a ceiling. Because you cannot see the layout, you cannot fuse an elementwise operation on A into the load, cannot do a custom epilogue on the accumulator without storing to shared memory first, and cannot exploit the fact that a Hopper fragment differs from an Ampere one. WMMA on Ampere supports 16x16x16, 32x8x16 and 8x32x16 for fp16 and bf16, plus 16x16x8 for tf32. The next step is `mma.sync` PTX, where the layout is documented per shape; CUTLASS and Triton both go there and reach cuBLAS-class throughput, which WMMA does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel calls load_matrix_sync inside `if (threadIdx.x < {n})`. Why is that wrong?
L4.answer: Fragment operations are warp-collective: all 32 lanes must execute them, because the tile is distributed across the warp's registers. Calling them under a lane-divergent branch is undefined behaviour.
L4.explanation: A fragment has no single owning thread; each lane holds a private, unspecified subset of the tile. Excluding lanes leaves parts of the tile unloaded and the mma reads whatever those registers held. The whole warp must participate in load, store, fill and mma.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need a fused epilogue applying a {op} to the accumulator before storing. WMMA or mma.sync?
options: WMMA, since fragment elements can be iterated with a.x[i]
mma.sync, because the per-lane accumulator layout is documented per shape and can be operated on directly
Neither; epilogues must always go through shared memory
L4.answer: mma.sync, because the per-lane accumulator layout is documented per shape and can be operated on directly
L4.explanation: WMMA exposes a.x[i] but leaves the index-to-element mapping unspecified, so touching it is undefined behaviour. The PTX mma.sync documentation gives an exact lane-and-register map per shape, which is what CUTLASS epilogues rely on. Shared-memory round trips work but cost bandwidth.

concepts.t: mma.sync, shapes and the fragment layout contract

L0.cloze: `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16` needs A in {{c1::4}} 32-bit registers per lane and B in {{c2::2}}; `{{c3::ldmatrix}}` exists precisely to load shared memory into that layout.

concepts.L1: `mma.sync` is the PTX instruction underneath everything. Unlike WMMA it publishes exactly which lane holds which matrix element for each shape, so you can construct fragments yourself, fuse into them, and control the shared-memory layout that feeds them.
concepts.L2: The layout is not row-major-in-registers, and rebuilding it by hand from shared memory produces a bank-conflict catastrophe. `ldmatrix` exists for this: it reads four 8x8 blocks in one instruction and distributes them into exactly the register pattern `mma.sync` expects.
concepts.L3: For `m16n8k16` with fp16 inputs, the 32 lanes hold a 16x16 A tile as 4 registers each: $32 \times 4 \times 2 = 256$ halves, exactly $16 \times 16$. B is 16x8, so $32 \times 2 \times 2 = 128$ halves, exactly $16 \times 8$. The fp32 accumulator is 16x8: $32 \times 4 = 128$ floats. The published map gives lane $l$ row $l/4$ and a column group from $l \bmod 4$, so the natural shared read is a strided gather that naively costs an 8-way bank conflict. `ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x4` does the permutation in hardware, which is why serious kernels pair a swizzled shared layout with `ldmatrix`. Consult the PTX ISA table for your shape; the map differs by shape and input type.

L4.prompt_tpl: For mma.sync m16n8k{K} with fp16 inputs and fp32 accumulator, how many 32-bit registers per lane hold A, B and C, and does the total match the tile sizes?
L4.answer: A: 4 regs (8 halves) per lane, 32*8 = 256 = 16*K. B: 2 regs (4 halves), 32*4 = 128 = K*8. C: 4 fp32 regs, 32*4 = 128 = 16*8.
L4.explanation: Every element of each tile lives in exactly one lane's register, so lanes times elements per lane must equal the tile size. A is 16 by 16 = 256 halves over 32 lanes = 8 halves = 4 registers each; B is 16 by 8 = 128 halves = 2 registers; C is 16 by 8 fp32 = 4 registers.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does a hand-written shared-memory load of the m{M}n8k16 A fragment hit bank conflicts, and what removes them?
L4.answer: The required per-lane pattern is strided, so groups of lanes land in the same banks. ldmatrix performs the permutation in hardware, and a swizzled shared layout keeps it conflict-free.
L4.explanation: The published map gives lane l a row derived from l/4, so four consecutive lanes read the same row region and lanes 4 apart read the same column offset, which collides in a row-major tile. ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x4 reads four 8x8 blocks and distributes them directly, replacing the whole gather.

L0.cloze: Hopper's `wgmma.mma_async` is issued by a {{c1::warpgroup}} of 4 warps, reads operands from {{c2::shared}} memory via descriptors, and completes {{c3::asynchronously}} against a wait_group.

concepts.L1: Hopper made the matrix instruction asynchronous and widened its issuer to a warpgroup of 128 threads. Operands are named by shared-memory descriptors rather than loaded into registers first, and completion is awaited explicitly, so the math unit runs concurrently with the copies feeding it.
concepts.L2: Asynchrony changes the program structure, not just the instruction. Once copies and math complete out of band, the efficient shape is producer-consumer: some warps issue TMA copies and signal mbarriers, others wait and issue `wgmma`. A uniform block cannot keep either unit busy.
concepts.L3: The dependency chain in a synchronous GEMM is copy, barrier, math, barrier, repeat, and the SM idles during each phase it is not in. Warp specialisation breaks the chain: with $k$ shared-memory stages, producer warps run ahead filling buffers $i+1 \ldots i+k-1$ while consumer warpgroups compute on buffer $i$, and the two only meet at an mbarrier. Because a TMA copy is one instruction and `wgmma` reads shared memory directly, the producer needs very few issue slots, so the split is cheap. Register allocation becomes asymmetric, which is why Hopper adds `setmaxnreg` to hand registers from producers to consumers. This structure is what FlashAttention-3 and Hopper CUTLASS are built from.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a warp-specialised kernel with {p} producer warps and {c} consumer warpgroups, explain what setmaxnreg is for.
L4.answer: Producers need almost no registers (they issue TMA copies), consumers need many (accumulators). setmaxnreg deallocates registers from producer warps and reallocates them to consumers, so the register file is not split evenly by default.
L4.explanation: Without it, every warp in the block gets the same register allocation, so the producer warps sit on registers they never use while the consumer accumulator tile is forced smaller or spills. Hopper exposes explicit per-warpgroup register redistribution to fix exactly this.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does wgmma take its A and B operands from shared memory descriptors rather than from registers, as mma.sync m16n8k{K} did?
options: Shared memory is faster than registers on Hopper
It removes the register-file staging and the ldmatrix step from the critical path, so the copy engine can feed the math unit directly
Registers cannot hold bf16 values
L4.answer: It removes the register-file staging and the ldmatrix step from the critical path, so the copy engine can feed the math unit directly
L4.explanation: With register operands, every tile must be loaded into registers by ldmatrix before the mma, consuming issue slots and register file. Descriptor operands let TMA land a tile in shared memory and wgmma consume it in place, which is what makes the producer-consumer split worthwhile.
